input.description: Show worktree source and list files
Show git-auth and config, find usages

input.command: cat -n src/routes.ts; cat package.json; git status --short

input.reason: I read src/worktree.ts, src/git-auth.ts, src/config.ts and src/routes.ts. `registerRepo` (routes.ts:19-22) takes `remoteUrl` from `req.body` and checks only that it is non-empty before calling `cloneRepo`. `cloneRepo` (worktree.ts:15) passes that URL and `SERVICE_TOKEN` (config.ts:4, which is `HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN`) to `gitAuthArgs`. `gitAuthArgs` (git-auth.ts:8) does have a guard, but it is only a substring check, `remoteUrl.includes("github.com")`. When the substring appears, it adds an `Authorization: Bearer` header through `http.extraHeader`. A URL such as `https://github.com.attacker.tld/x`, or one with `github.com` in its path, therefore gets the token sent to the attacker's host. So the leak is real. The finding goes too far, though, when it says the token goes to "whatever host the URL names". URLs without that substring get no auth args at all.
input.summary: cloneRepo sends the service token to any host whose URL contains github.com

findings.text: `cloneRepo` passes the user-supplied `remoteUrl` straight to `gitAuthArgs` with the service token, so `git clone` sends the token to any host whose URL contains the substring `github.com`.
findings.reason: The central claim holds. `remoteUrl` comes straight from `req.body` with only a non-empty check (routes.ts:19-22), and `cloneRepo` passes it with `SERVICE_TOKEN` to `gitAuthArgs` (worktree.ts:15). The claim that the token goes to "whatever host the URL names" is too broad. `gitAuthArgs` returns the Authorization header only when `remoteUrl.includes("github.com")` and returns `[]` otherwise. The token therefore reaches an arbitrary host only when that host's URL contains the substring, e.g. `github.com.attacker.tld` or a path containing `github.com`. That still makes it exploitable. The final clause is narrowed to match the guard.

input.severity_reason: This is an exploitable credential leak. Any user who can call registerRepo can send a URL such as `https://github.com.attacker.tld/x`. That gets the service's GitHub bearer token sent to a server the attacker controls. The attacker can then use the service's GitHub access.
